analysis.one_liner: Bars homebuilders from forcing homebuyers into mandatory arbitration to buy a new house.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many builders of new homes write a clause into the purchase contract requiring buyers to settle any dispute with a private arbitrator instead of going to court, often before the buyer even signs. This bill would make it illegal to require that agreement as a condition of buying a new house, would force any arbitration agreement into its own separate document with a plain warning that signing means giving up the right to go to court, and would let buyers help pick the arbitrator after a dispute actually arises. It died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying a newly built home, who would keep the right to sue in court over construction defects and would not have to waive that right just to close the deal.

how_it_helps.text: Builders could not make arbitration a condition precedent to signing a home purchase contract, so a buyer could buy a house without waiving court access [S2][S3].

Any arbitration agreement would have to be a separate document containing only arbitration terms, with the warning: "By Agreeing to Binding Arbitration You Are Giving Up Your Right To Go To Court" [S3].
The agreement could not pre-name an arbitrator and would have to guarantee the buyer a role in selecting one, chosen only after a dispute has arisen [S3].
A builder who violated these rules would lose the ability to enforce the arbitration agreement at all [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Homebuilders, who would lose the leverage of presenting arbitration as a take-it-or-leave-it part of the standard purchase contract, and the arbitration industry, which would see fewer consumer contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban mandatory arbitration in home sales outright; a builder could still offer a separate standalone arbitration agreement, so buyers signing quickly could still waive court rights [S3].
Supporters of arbitration argue it can be faster and cheaper than court for construction disputes, and the bill would add contract paperwork and legal uncertainty for builders and buyers alike [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but modest: it targets the most coercive practice — burying arbitration in the purchase contract — rather than eliminating arbitration. The cost falls on builders' contract practices, not on home prices in any way the record documents. The bill's larger problem is that it never moved at all, so neither its benefits nor its costs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its Housing subcommittee, where it sat until the 109th Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Gonzalez introduced the bill on October 7, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
On January 4, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity, where it remained with no further action [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and never advanced past committee before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuilders keep the ability to require arbitration as a standard part of new-home contracts, and buyers continue to sign away court access to close on a house.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Homebuilders, and homebuyers keep waiving court rights

for.name: Rep. Charles A. Gonzalez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Homebuyers Protection Act; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Michael Oxley, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Housing and Community Opportunity Subcommittee on January 4, 2006, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no committee or floor vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: Builders use arbitration clauses in standard purchase contracts to channel disputes with buyers into private arbitration, away from court. The bill would strip that leverage; since it died, nothing changed for them.

Arbitration providers depend on mandatory clauses in consumer contracts for volume. Fewer homebuyers forced into arbitration means fewer paying disputes; the bill never advanced, so their business was untouched.
